source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα δ᾿ ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐπιστάμενος δέκα εἶπεν ἢ ἕνδεκά τινας ἐξαρτησάμενον τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἑαυτῷ ἐπιῤῥήτους ἀνθρώπους, τελώνας καὶ ναύτας τοὺς πονηροτάτους, μετὰ τούτων τῇδε κἀκεῖσε αὐτὸν ἀποδεδρακέναι, αἰσχρῶς καὶ γλίσχρως τροφὰς συνάγοντα, φέρε καὶ περὶ τούτων κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν διαλάβωμεν. φανερὸν δέ ἐστι τοῖς ἐντυγχάνουσιν εὐαγγελικοῖς λόγοις, οὓς οὐδ᾿ ἀνεγνωκέναι ὁ Κέλσος φαίνεται, ὅτι δώδεκα ἀποστόλους ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπελέξατο, τελώνην μὲν τὸν Ματθαῖον, οὓς δ᾿ εἶπε συγκεχυμένως ναύτας τάχα τὸν Ἰάκωβον καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην φησὶν, ἐπεὶ καταλιπόντες τὸ πλοῖον καὶ „τὸν πατέρα αὐτῶν Ζεβεδαῖον“ ἠκολούθησαν τῷ Ἰησοῦ. τὸν γὰρ Πέτρον καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ Ἀνδρέαν, ἀμφιβλήστρῳ χρωμένους διὰ τὰς ἀναγκαίας τροφὰς, οὐκ ἐν ναύταις ἀλλ᾿, ὡς ἀνέγραψεν ἡ γραφὴ, ἐν ἁλιεῦσιν ἀριθμητέον. ἔστω δὲ καὶ ὁ Λευὴς τελώνης ἀκολουθήσας τῷ Ἰησοῦ· ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῶν ἀποστόλων αὐτοῦ ἦν εἰ μὴ κατά τινα τῶν ἀντιγράφων τοῦ κατὰ Μάρκον εὐαγγελίου. τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οὐ μεμαθήκαμεν τὰ ἔργα, ὅθεν πρὸ τῆς μαθητείας τοῦ Ἰησοῦ περιεποίουν ἑαυτοῖς τὰς τροφάς. φημὶ οὖν καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα ὅτι τοῖς δυναμένοις φρονίμως καὶ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξετάζειν τὰ περὶ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦ Ἰησοῦ φαίνεται ὅτι δυνάμει θείᾳ ἐδίδασκον οὗτοι τὸν χριστιανισμὸν καὶ ἐπετύγχανον ὑπάγοντες ἀνθρώπους τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ. οὐ γὰρ ἡ εἰς τὸ λέγειν δύναμις καὶ τάξις ἀπαγγελίας κατὰ τὰς Ἑλλήνων διαλεκτικὰς ἢ ῥητορικὰς τέχνας ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς ὑπαγομένη τοὺς ἀκούοντας. δοκεῖ δέ μοι ὅτι σοφοὺς μέν τινας ὡς πρὸς τὴν τῶν πολλῶν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ἱκανοὺς πρὸς τὸ νοεῖν ἀρεσκόντως πλήθεσι καὶ λέγειν ἐπιλεξάμενος καὶ χρησάμενος αὐτοῖς διακόνοις τῆς διδασκαλίας ὁ Ἰησοῦς εὐλογώτατ᾿ ἂν ὑπενοήθη ὁμοίᾳ φιλοσόφοις κεκηρύχθαι ἀγωγῇ, αἱρέσεώς τινος προϊσταμένοις· καὶ οὐκέτ᾿ ἂν ἡ περὶ τοῦ θεῖον εἶναι τον λόγον ἐπαγγελία ἀνεφαίνετο, ἅτε τοῦ λόγου ὄντος καὶ τοῦ κηρύγματος ἐν πειθοῖς τῆς ἐν φράσει καὶ συνθέσει τῶν λέξεων σοφίας· καὶ ἦν ἂν „ἡ πίστις“ ὁμοίως τῇ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου φιλοσόφων περὶ τῶν δογμάτων πίστει „ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων“ καὶ οὐκ „ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ“· νυνὶ δὲ τίς βλέπων ἁλιεῖς καὶ τελώνας μηδὲ τὰ πρῶτα γράμματα μεμαθηκότας (ὡς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἀναγράφει περὶ αὐτῶν καὶ ὁ Κέλσος κατὰ ταῦτα πεπίστευκεν αὐτοῖς, ἀληθεύουσι περὶ τῆς ἰδιωτείας αὐτῶν), τεθαῤῥηκότως οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις ὁμιλοῦντας περὶ τῆς εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν πίστεως ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσι κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν καὶ ἀνύοντας, οὐκ ἂν ζητήσαι, πόθεν ἦν αὐτοῖς δύναμις πειστική; οὐ γὰρ ἡ νενομισμένη τοῖς πολλοῖς. καὶ τίς οὐκ ἂν λέγοι ὅτι τὸ „δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου, καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων“ δυνάμει τινὶ θείᾳ ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ ἐπλήρωσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς; ἥντινα καὶ ὁ Παῦλος παριστὰς, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν, φησί· „καὶ ὁ λόγος μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμά μου οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις ἀλλ᾿ ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, ἵν᾿ ἡ πίστις ἡμῶν μὴ ᾖ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἁνθρώπων ἀλλ᾿ ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ.“ κατὰ γὰρ τὰ εἰρημένα ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, προγνωστικῶς ἀπαγγέλλουσι περὶ τῆς κηρύξεως τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, „κύριος ἔδωκε ῥῆμα τοῖς εὐαγγελιζομένοις δυνάμει πολλῇ, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν δυνάμεων τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ,“ ἵνα καὶ ἡ λέγουσα προφητεία· „ἕως τάχους δραμεῖται ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ“ πληρωθῇ. καὶ βλέπομέν γε ὅτι „εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ“ τῶν ἀποστόλων Ἰησοῦ „φθόγγος, καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν.“ διὰ τοῦτο δυνάμεως μὲν πληροῦνται οἱ λόγου τοῦ μετὰ δυνάμεως ἀπαγγελλομένου ἀκούοντες, ἣν ἐπιδείκνυνται τῇ τε διαθέσει καὶ τῷ βίῳ καὶ τῷ ἕως θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας· διάκενοι δέ τινες εἰσὶ, κἂν ἐπαγγέλλωνται πιστεύειν τῷ θεῷ διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, οἱ μὴ δύναμιν θείαν ἔχοντες προσάγεσθαι δοκοῦντες τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ. εἰ καὶ ἀνωτέρω δ᾿ ἐμνήσθην εὐαγγελικοῦ ῥητοῦ ὑπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος εἰρημένου, οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ νῦν αὐτῷ κατὰ καιρὸν χρήσομαι, παριστὰς καὶ τὴν τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν περὶ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου κηρύξεως πρόγνωσιν θειότατα δηλουμένην καὶ τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἰσχὺν, χωρὶς διδασκάλων κρατοῦσαν τῶν πιστευόντων τῇ μετὰ δυνάμεως θείας πειθοῖ. φησὶ δὴ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· „ὁ μὲν θερισμὸς πολὺς, οἱ δὲ ἐργάται ὀλίγοι· δεήθητε οὖν τοῦ κυρίου τοῦ θερισμοῦ, ὅπως ἐκβάλῃ ἐργάτας εἰς τὸν θερισμὸν αὐτοῦ.“
pass_a_gloss: After these things, since he did not even know the number of the apostles, he said ten or eleven, having attached to himself uneducated men, tax collectors and sailors, the most wicked, with whom he went here and there, gathering food shamefully and filthily. Let us also examine these things as much as possible. It is clear to those who examine the evangelical words, which Celsus seems not to have read, that Jesus chose twelve apostles, a tax collector, Matthew, and perhaps those he called sailors, James and John, since they left their boat and their father Zebedee and followed Jesus. For Peter and his brother Andrew, using a fishing net for necessary food, should not be counted among sailors but, as the scripture wrote, among fishermen. Let it be that Levi, the tax collector, also followed Jesus, but he was not one of the number of his apostles, unless according to some manuscripts of the Gospel of Mark. We have not learned what the others did before they became disciples of Jesus to provide for themselves. I say, therefore, that to those who can examine wisely and gratefully the things about the apostles of Jesus, it appears that they taught Christianity with divine power and persuaded people to follow the word of God. For it was not the power of speaking and the order of proclamation according to Greek dialectics or rhetorical skills that was in them, leading those who listened. It seems to me that Jesus, having chosen some wise men, as it were, according to the opinion of the many and sufficient to think and speak pleasingly to the crowds, and having used them as servants of his teaching, would have been thought blessed to have proclaimed a similar philosophical education, presiding over some sect. And the promise about the divine word would not have been revealed, since the word and the proclamation were in the persuasions of human wisdom in the phrase and composition of words. And faith would have been similar to the faith of the philosophers of this world regarding their doctrines, in human wisdom and not in the power of God. Now, who seeing fishermen and tax collectors, not even having learned the first letters, as the gospel writes about them and Celsus has believed them, telling the truth about their private lives, would not have wondered at their boldly speaking not only to Jews about faith in Jesus but also proclaiming him to the other nations and enduring, and would not have asked where they got their persuasive power, since it was not the customary one among the many? And who would not say that Jesus fulfilled his statement, 'Come after me, and I will make you fishermen of men,' with some divine power in his apostles? Which Paul also presents, as we said above, saying, 'My word and my proclamation were not in persuasions of human wisdom but in demonstration of spirit and power, so that our faith may not be in human wisdom but in the power of God.' For according to what was said by the prophets, who proclaim the proclamation of the gospel with foreknowledge, 'The Lord gave a word to those proclaiming with great power, the king of powers of the beloved,' so that the prophecy saying, 'His word will run swiftly,' may be fulfilled. And we see that 'their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.' Therefore, those who hear the word proclaimed with power are filled with power, which they demonstrate by their disposition and life and their struggle for the truth even to death. But some are servants who, even if they promise to believe in God through Jesus, seem not to have divine power to bring people to the word of God. Although I mentioned above the evangelical saying spoken by the Savior, I will use it again now, presenting the Savior's most divine foreknowledge about the proclamation of the gospel and the power of the word, which holds those who believe in it with divine power, without teachers. Jesus says, 'The harvest is great, but the workers are few; therefore, ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.'

pass_b_english: After all this, since Celsus does not even know how many apostles there were — he says ten or eleven — he claims Jesus attached uneducated men to himself, tax collectors and sailors, the most wicked sort, and went here and there with them, gathering food shamefully and filthily. We should examine these points as best we can. Anyone who reads the Gospels can see that Jesus chose twelve apostles, a fact Celsus appears not to have read. Matthew was a tax collector. As for the ones Celsus vaguely calls sailors, they are probably James and John, since they left their boat and their father Zebedee to follow Jesus (Matthew 4:19). Peter and his brother Andrew used a fishing net to earn their necessary food; Scripture counts them as fishermen, not sailors. Let us grant that Levi the tax collector also followed Jesus, but he was not numbered among the apostles unless one follows certain manuscripts of Mark’s Gospel. We do not know what the rest did for a living before becoming disciples. I say, then, that anyone able to examine the apostles wisely and fairly will see they taught Christianity with divine power and persuaded people to follow the word of God. It was not skill in speaking or a polished rhetorical technique modeled on Greek dialectic or rhetoric that drew their hearers. In my judgment, if Jesus had chosen men considered wise by popular opinion, men capable of thinking and speaking pleasingly to crowds, and had used them as servants of his teaching, he would have been thought to have established a philosophical school like any other sect. The claim that the word is divine would not have appeared, because the word and the proclamation would have rested on the persuasions of human wisdom in phrasing and composition. Faith would have been like the faith of this world’s philosophers in their doctrines — in human wisdom, not in the power of God (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). But now, who sees fishermen and tax collectors who had not even learned their letters — as the Gospel records and Celsus accepts, attesting to their obscurity — speaking boldly not only to Jews about faith in Jesus but also proclaiming him among the nations and succeeding, and would not ask where their persuasive power came from, since it was not the ordinary kind? Who would not say that Jesus fulfilled his word, ‘Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,’ by divine power in his apostles (Matthew 4:19)? Paul confirms this, as we said earlier: ‘My speech and my proclamation were not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God’ (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). For the prophets foretold the gospel’s proclamation: ‘The Lord gave the word; great was the company of those who published it, the King of the powers of the Beloved,’ so that the prophecy ‘His word runs swiftly’ might be fulfilled (Psalm 68:11). And we see that ‘their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’ (Psalm 19:4). Therefore those who hear the word proclaimed with power are filled with that power, which they show by their character, their life, and their struggle for the truth even to death. But some are empty: even if they claim to believe in God through Jesus, they seem to lack the divine power that draws people to the word of God. Although I cited the Savior’s Gospel saying earlier, I will use it again now, because it displays his divine foreknowledge about the gospel’s proclamation and the power of the word that holds believers fast without human teachers. Jesus says, ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest’ (Matthew 9:37–38).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A preserves all clauses and nuances. Pass B provides appropriate scripture citations (Matthew 4:19, 1 Corinthians 2:4–5, Psalm 68:11, Psalm 19:4, Matthew 9:37–38) which correspond to the Greek allusions/quotes. The distinction between 'sailors' (ναύτας) and 'fishermen' (ἁλιεῦσιν) is maintained. The translation of 'ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις' as 'in persuasions of human wisdom' is faithful.
